title: Two cities, one bridge
summary: A woman visits the town on the other side of the river for the first time in fifty years.
paragraphs: For fifty-two years, Dolores had lived in a town on one side of a wide river. On the other side, so close that she could see the church tower from her kitchen window, was another town in another country. There had always been a bridge, but for most of her life there had also been a {{border}}, with {{guards}}, passports and long queues. As a child she had been told that the other side was different, and somehow she had never gone.

Then the border controls ended. At first nothing changed for Dolores. She was used to her side: her market, her bakery, her friends. But her granddaughter, Mía, who was fifteen and curious about everything, kept asking. "Grandma, have you really never been? It's ten minutes away!" One Sunday in May, Dolores finally agreed.

They walked across the bridge slowly. In the middle, Dolores stopped and looked at the water. "My father used to fish here," she said. "Fishermen from both sides met in the middle of the river and exchanged cigarettes and news. On land they weren't allowed to talk, but on the water nobody was watching."

The other town was smaller than she expected and, in many ways, very {{familiar}}. The houses had the same red roofs. The old women in the market argued about the price of tomatoes in exactly the same way. The words were different, but many were similar, and Mía, who was studying the language at school, translated for her. In a café near the church, an old man heard Dolores's {{accent}} and asked where she was from. When she told him, he smiled. "My mother was from your town," he said. "She crossed the bridge to marry my father, in 1958."

They talked for two hours. When Dolores and Mía walked back across the bridge, the sun was setting behind the church tower. "Next week," Dolores said, "we'll go again. I want to see the market on a Saturday." Mía laughed. "Fifty-two years, and now you're in a hurry?" Dolores smiled. "That," she said, "is exactly why I'm in a hurry."

border.meaning: the official line between two countries

guards.meaning: people whose job is to watch a place and control who goes in

familiar.meaning: known to you, easy to recognise

accent.meaning: the way a person pronounces words, which shows where they come from

questions.question: Why had Dolores never visited the other town?
options: There had been a border, and she was used to her own side.
questions.explanation: For most of her life there had been a border, and she was used to her own side.

questions.question: What did Dolores's father do in the middle of the river?
options: He met fishermen from the other side and exchanged news.
He crossed into the other country.
He worked as a border guard.
questions.explanation: Fishermen from both sides met in the middle and exchanged cigarettes and news.

questions.question: How did Dolores find the other town?
options: Smaller than expected and very familiar
questions.explanation: It was smaller than she expected and, in many ways, very familiar.

questions.question: What does Dolores mean at the end?
options: She wants to move to the other town.
She waited so long that now she doesn't want to waste time.
She is tired and wants to go home.
She will never cross the bridge again.
questions.explanation: Because she waited fifty-two years, she is now in a hurry.
